detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A biological, chemical or physical agent in food, or a condition of food, with the potential to cause an adverse health effect
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual reproduces the Codex formulation: a hazard is an agent or condition with the potential to cause an adverse health effect. The word “potential” matters; actual illness need not already have occurred.

why_other_options_are_incorrect.B: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Any defect that reduces the commercial value of food.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.C: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Any organism that causes visible spoilage.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.D: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Only a chemical contaminant present above a legal limit.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Toxicity is the capacity to cause harm; hazard depends on the circumstances of exposure and use
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual treats toxicity as an intrinsic capacity of a substance and hazard as contextual, affected by dose, exposure route and conditions of use. A toxic substance may pose a low practical hazard when appropriately controlled.

why_other_options_are_incorrect.A: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Toxicity and hazard are interchangeable terms.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.C: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Hazard is an intrinsic property, while toxicity depends only on food price.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.D: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Toxicity applies only to biological agents.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Rodent droppings or visible insect larvae
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Macro-biological hazards are visible pests or pest-related matter such as larvae, adult insects, rodent droppings and hair. Salmonella is microbiological; aflatoxin and mercury are chemical hazards.

why_other_options_are_incorrect.A: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Salmonella cells.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.B: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Aflatoxin.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.D: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Mercury.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Viruses may survive in food and be transmitted through it, but do not multiply in food
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The module identifies viruses as microbiological hazards that can survive in food and transmit by the faecal–oral route, but do not multiply in food itself.

why_other_options_are_incorrect.A: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Viruses multiply rapidly in all refrigerated foods.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.B: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Viruses are classified as physical hazards.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.C: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Viruses can only be transmitted through cooked food.

detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The module lists Pb, Hg, As and Cd as heavy-metal environmental pollutants. It links their entry to industrial discharge and accumulation through the food chain.

why_other_options_are_incorrect.B: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Physical hazards.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.C: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Macro-biological hazards.
why_other_options_are_incorrect.D: This option does not match the concept or fact tested: Food quality indicators.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Food intoxication
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Intoxication results from ingesting a toxin already present in food; multiplication or invasion by the organism in the consumer is not required. The module contrasts this with infection caused by live pathogens.
